name: legged-locomotion
title: Legged Locomotion — a CTRNN Central Pattern Generator (Beer & Gallagher 1992)
lead:
This is the rhythmic-behaviour brain-body-environment model. Unlike the
chemotaxis and discrimination agents, which react to an external stimulus,
the walker must GENERATE its own temporal structure: a periodic motor pattern
that persists. The scientific payoff is the CPG limit cycle — a closed loop in
the network's state space — and the gait it produces (stride period, duty
factor, velocity), read directly off the coupled dynamics.

at_a_glance.role: the agent walks steadily forward (distance + monotone progress)
the CPG's rhythmic dynamics: the CTRNN state's limit cycle
the gait quantified: stride period, duty factor, mean velocity

glossary.definition: A neural circuit that produces a rhythmic motor pattern without needing rhythmic input — here, the evolved CTRNN's self-sustaining cycle.
A closed, attracting loop in a dynamical system's state space — the mathematical form of a stable rhythm.
Stance: foot planted, leg driving the body forward. Swing: foot lifted, leg recovering forward for the next step.
The fraction of a stride the foot is on the ground (in stance). ~0.5 means stance and swing take about equal time.
The number of time-steps between successive foot-plant onsets — the gait's cycle length.
The agent's sense of its own leg angle, fed back to the CTRNN so the CPG can be sensory-entrained.

biological_story:
Walking is not a reflex to a stimulus — it is a rhythm an animal makes for
itself. A leg must push against the ground to drive the body forward, then
lift and reach ahead to do it again, over and over, in time. Beer & Gallagher
asked whether the smallest kind of nervous system — a handful of
continuously-interacting neurons — could invent that rhythm on its own when
evolution rewards getting somewhere. It can. The evolved network here does not
step on a metronome; its neurons settle into a self-sustaining cycle, a loop in
their own activity that repeats about every twenty time-steps. On each loop the
motor neurons plant the foot and sweep the leg back — the body lurches forward —
then lift the foot and sweep forward to set up the next step. Read off the
network's state, that cycle is a closed ring: the central pattern generator's
attractor. The leg, the ground, and the little brain together make a walker.
question:
Can a small continuous-time recurrent neural network, coupled to a single
leg over flat ground, evolve into a central pattern generator that produces
a rhythmic walking gait — a self-sustaining stance/swing cycle that carries
the body steadily forward — rather than a one-off lunge?
hypothesis:
A CTRNN evolved to maximize forward travel, with its leg angle fed back as
proprioception, will settle into a stable limit cycle: it plants the foot and
swings the leg backward to drive the body forward (stance), lifts and swings
forward to recover (swing), and repeats. The rhythm is a dynamical attractor
of the coupled brain-body system, not a scripted sequence — the signature of
a central pattern generator.

executive.what_is_this:
An evolved 5-neuron CTRNN (one neuron receives the leg-angle proprioceptive
input; three motor neurons drive foot up/down, backward-swing and
forward-swing) driving a single clean-room leg over flat ground. When the
planted foot swings backward the body translates forward; when the foot
lifts the leg swings freely to recover. The genome was evolved by the
workspace's own GA and committed; the studies replay it deterministically.
executive.verdict:
Reproduced. The evolved CTRNN is a genuine central pattern generator: it
walks forward ~450 units over a 500-step trial with a REGULAR gait — 25
strides of period 19.8 ± 0.4 steps, duty factor 0.44 — and its state traces
a clean limit cycle. It never reverses at stride scale (only sub-0.3-unit
coasting jitter; net strictly forward). This is rhythmic locomotion from a
small neural dynamical system, exactly the Beer & Gallagher result.
executive.verdict_detail:
From the committed seed (CTRNN size 5, pop 80, gen 120, seed 0), verified in
the test suite: distance > 200 (achieved 450.7), ≥ 10 foot cycles (achieved
25), duty factor in the walking band (achieved 0.44), and a regular stride
period (19.8 ± 0.4 steps). Honest scope + tuning: a pure net-distance
fitness evolves a DEGENERATE single lunge (one plant, then coast — distance
~21, no stride cycle). An opt-in rhythm-shaped fitness — distance scaled by
the number of PRODUCTIVE strides (stance phases that actually advance the
body, so marching in place earns nothing) — was needed to evolve a true
rhythmic gait. Pure distance remains the faithful default; the shaping is the
documented choice that makes a walk learnable.

decisions_needed.question: Report the single evolved walker (as the paper analyzes one CPG), or sweep leg geometry / omega-gain to map the gaits that evolve?
decisions_needed.context: Beer & Gallagher analyze one evolved walker's dynamics in depth. A geometry sweep is a documented extension.

scientific_argument.main_claim:
Rhythmic walking here is a dynamical property of the coupled brain-body
system: a small CTRNN, with proprioceptive feedback, settles into a stable
limit cycle whose period and phase organize a stance/swing gait — a central
pattern generator, with no clock or scripted step sequence.
evidence_for: Walks forward ~450 units over 500 steps, net strictly forward (no stride-scale reversal; figures/walk.gif, test_walker_seed.py).
A regular gait: 25 strides of period 19.8 ± 0.4 steps, duty factor 0.44 (figures/gait_diagram.png).
The CTRNN state traces a closed limit cycle — the CPG attractor (figures/cpg_limit_cycle.png).
The rhythm emerges over evolution (figures/evolution_curves.png): distance and regularity climb across generations.
evidence_against: A pure net-distance fitness does NOT evolve a walk — it finds a single lunge; the rhythmic gait required a rhythm-shaped fitness (documented, opt-in).
key_figures: figures/walk.gif — the leg stepping and the body advancing (the walk in motion)
figures/cpg_limit_cycle.png — the CTRNN state's limit cycle (the CPG attractor)
figures/gait_diagram.png — stance/swing bands + leg angle + body velocity (stride period, duty factor)
figures/neural_activity.gif — the CPG's firing pattern driving the leg
caveats: Fitness used an opt-in rhythm-shaping term; pure net distance is the faithful default (and evolves a lunge, not a walk).
Clean-room leg constants (leg_length 15, angle range ±π/6, friction 0.9, dt 0.1): documented choices matching the Beer walker's structure, not fitted to data.
A single evolved walker is analyzed, as in the paper; a geometry/gain sweep is a documented extension.

studies.name: walk-forward
studies.title: The Walker Walks Forward
studies.question:
Does the evolved CTRNN drive the leg so the body travels steadily forward,
with a repeating step cycle rather than a single lunge?

findings.summary: Walks ~450 units in 500 steps with 25 steps; net strictly forward (sub-0.3-unit coasting jitter only); a pure-distance fitness instead evolves a single ~21-unit lunge.
findings.detail:
figures/walk.gif shows the leg planting and swinging as the body advances
across the ground; figures/gait_diagram.png shows the stance/swing bands and
the steadily rising body position/velocity.

studies.claim:
The evolved walker travels ~450 units over a 500-step trial and never
reverses, taking 25 regular steps — a sustained forward walk, not a one-off
lunge (which a pure-distance fitness produces, reaching only ~21).

derived.insight: Walks ~450 units in 500 steps with 25 steps; net strictly forward (sub-0.3-unit coasting jitter only); a pure-distance fitness instead evolves a single ~21-unit lunge.

studies.name: cpg-limit-cycle
studies.title: The CPG's Limit Cycle
studies.question:
Is the walking rhythm a dynamical attractor of the CTRNN — does the network's
state trace a stable closed loop (a limit cycle), the signature of a central
pattern generator?

findings.summary: The CTRNN state settles onto a closed limit cycle repeating once per stride — the CPG attractor.

studies.claim:
The evolved CTRNN's state traces a clean closed loop in its activity space — a
limit cycle — repeating once per stride (~19.8 steps). The rhythm is a
self-sustaining attractor, not a clocked or scripted sequence.

derived.insight: The CTRNN state settles onto a closed limit cycle repeating once per stride — the CPG attractor.

studies.name: gait-and-velocity
studies.title: Gait Quantified — Stride, Duty, Velocity
studies.question:
What gait does the evolved walker produce — how regular is its stride, how is
stance/swing balanced, and how fast does the body move?

findings.summary: Stride period 19.8 ± 0.4 steps, duty factor 0.44, mean velocity ~9.0 — a regular, balanced gait.
findings.detail:
figures/gait_diagram.png annotates the measured stride period and duty
factor on the stance/swing bands; figures/cpg_limit_cycle.png shows the
underlying regularity in the CTRNN state.

studies.claim:
A regular gait: stride period 19.8 ± 0.4 steps (the spread is only ~2% of the
period), duty factor 0.44 (stance and swing nearly balanced), mean body
velocity ~9.0 units/time (~0.9 units/step).

derived.insight: Stride period 19.8 ± 0.4 steps, duty factor 0.44, mean velocity ~9.0 — a regular, balanced gait.
